result.corrected_verdict: no (usable_in_vigilant). This is not an odds or scores source. It is a 15-line demo whose WebSocket sends random decimals every 3 seconds, with no upstream, no timestamp and no vendor, so it has no price age to beat CNO's 13-33 s cadence or the Novig makers' 16 s re-quote. It is free only because it carries no data. Its one idea, relaying a feed over a FastAPI WebSocket to browsers, is worse than what Vigilant already does (a single-user Android foreground service opening upstream sockets and REST polls directly): a relay adds a hop, a host to pay for and keep running, and up to 3 s of timer latency on top of the real feed's age. Nothing to build, nothing to test on the phone, nothing to spend credits on. The only open question worth asking is which upstream to connect, and this article does not answer it; that belongs to the other nine sources and the already-known list.

contrary_evidence.what: The best case for keeping the scout's 'technique-only': a small always-on relay could hold an upstream vendor key off the phone and let several devices share one socket. Weak for Vigilant: it is a single-user app, BRIEF.md and NOVIG_API.md already have the phone hold its own trading::read key, and a hosted relay costs money (INFERRED: always-on hosting is not free), adds a hop, and must sit on a network the phone does not control. The tutorial also shows no key handling beyond a python-dotenv import that nothing uses.

The RSS body is the full article and links nothing else, so there is no hidden second source (repo, vendor, API) behind the Cloudflare-blocked page that could change this verdict. Part 2 is announced but absent from the feed.

details.free_tier_limits: not found. There is no API, no plan and no quota; the tutorial calls no vendor. The only free things are the open-source packages it names (fastapi, uvicorn; the scout states they are free and open source, I did not read their licence texts). Medium's own RSS feed answered HTTP 200 with the full article body, no login. Reading the article page itself returned Cloudflare 403 from this container.
details.signup_friction: None for the tutorial: no account, key or card is requested anywhere. There is also no key to obtain because there is no data vendor. The only 'key' mention is a generic python-dotenv tip with nothing reading it.
details.us_sports_and_props_coverage: none. One hard-coded fake matchup 'Team A vs Team B' with two random decimals between 1.5 and 2.5 (random.uniform). No leagues, no US sports, no props, no in-play or pregame distinction, no scores. The intro mentions soccer events (goals, red cards) only as motivation.
details.sharp_books_or_exchanges_covered: none. No Pinnacle, Circa, Kalshi, ProphetX, Sporttrade, Novig or any other book or exchange is named anywhere in the article.
details.websocket_or_live_included_free: A WebSocket exists, but it is the author's own toy endpoint at ws://localhost:8000/ws/odds (VERIFIED from the article: 'You now have a live WebSocket server at ws://localhost:8000/ws/odds streaming randomized odds!'). It is not a hosted service, nothing is publicly reachable, and the stream is timer-driven random data every 3 s, so it carries no live odds and no live scores. Free because there is nothing there.
details.duplicates_what_the_app_already_has: It adds nothing and duplicates nothing real. It is not a reseller of any of the known sources (it resells nothing). Against the known list it is strictly worse than every entry (Polymarket sockets, Kalshi, Sofascore, ESPN, ParlayAPI, PropLine, PinnWire, The Odds API), since all of those carry real prices or scores. The only overlap is the generic pattern 'push a feed over a WebSocket', which Vigilant already uses against Novig's own websocket (NOVIG_API.md section 6) from a foreground service (BRIEF.md: ScanService, AutoScanService) with OkHttp.
details.android_phone_feasibility: No feed to read, so nothing for the phone to consume. Could Vigilant read it directly? There is nothing hosted to connect to; the endpoint exists only on the reader's own machine. Would it need a server? The pattern itself is a server (FastAPI, Python 3.9+); a phone would only ever be a client of it. Running one would mean either a hosted always-on box (INFERRED: a cost, a host to keep alive, an extra hop and a possible 3 s timer delay on top of the real feed's age) or Python-on-Android (INFERRED: pointless, as the app can already call upstream sockets and REST polls itself). Rate, battery and key storage: moot, as nothing is polled and no key exists. Network block: the Cloudflare 403 seen here applies only to Medium's HTML pages (and its ToS/licence pages), not to any data feed, and Vigilant would never read Medium at runtime, so the phone-versus-container network question does not arise.
